newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Transit gas not hit by Russia-Ukraine dispute - MOL.
newsitem.headline: Transit gas not hit by Russia-Ukraine dispute - MOL.

text.p: The current energy payments dispute between Russia and the Ukraine which reduced gas supplies to Ukraine by one-third this week has not affected transit supplies to Europe, Hungary's oil and gas company MOL said.
"We are working without problem, this decrease in volume was only for Ukraine's own supplies and transit supplies were unaffected," a MOL official told Reuters on Friday.
"Today we are receiving the contracted volume of 1,300,000 cubic metres per second."
Russia's giant gas company Gazprom sends all its supplies to Europe through Ukraine and on through a main pipeline via Slovakia and a smaller one through Hungary to Austria.

Ukraine and Russian gas monopoly RAO Gazprom are currently caught in a complex game of supply cuts, urgent meetings and secretive commercial talks -- all overshadowed by suspicions of Moscow's imperialistic intentions.

Gazprom chief Rem Vyakhirev held talks in Kiev on Wednesday with President Leonid Kuchma, his prime minister and the upper echelons of the State Oil and Gas Committee after his company cut supplies by one-third to Ukraine this week.
Ukraine owes Gazprom $3.5 billion for 1992-94 supplies, including $1.4 billion already restructured for 12 years with the first $221.5 million tranche to be paid by the end of 1997.

Gazprom said earlier in a statement that despite cuts to the two largest privately-owned Ukrainian importers, the company would continue to supply gas under an existing contract so Ukraine's strategic resources could keep running.
The MOL official said that according to his company's information Vyakhirev had agreed following his visit to Kiev to restore all gas supplies to their normal levels.
"We heard that there was about a 40 percent decrease but after Mr Vyakhirev was in Kiev they decided that they would resume the supplies," he said.
The official added that if transit supplies were cut Hungary had enough gas reserves to last three to four months.
According to MOL figures, Hungary used 11.68 billion cubic metres of natural gas in 1995, of which 6.8 billion was imported, mainly from Russia.
MOL signed a contract with gas importer Panrusgaz last November for the delivery of 225 billion cubic metres of Russian natural gas to Hungary over 20 years.
MOL is Panrusgaz's only customer in Hungary, as only MOL has gas distribution rights in the country. Deliveries agreed in the present contract are guaranteed by Gazprom.
MOL is 58 percent owned by Hungary's state privatisation agency APV Rt, with foreign investors holding 30 percent.
On the Budapest Stock Exchange MOL shares closed up 50 om Fridat at 4,355.
